findings.title: New abstract order() method breaks every existing CryptoProvider implementation
findings.body: `int order();` is added as an abstract interface method with no default. Any existing implementor outside the modified files (third-party providers, test doubles, other modules not in this PR) will fail to compile, and any that is loaded at runtime will fail with AbstractMethodError. A `default` returning a fixed value (for example the current behaviour, or a lower priority) would keep the contract backward compatible.

findings.title: Providers with equal order() are chosen arbitrarily instead of failing
findings.body: Previously more than one CryptoProvider on the classpath raised an IllegalStateException. Now the list is sorted only by order(), and providers with the same order (DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider and FIPS1402Provider all return 200) keep ServiceLoader iteration order, which is not defined. Two providers with the same priority can therefore be picked nondeterministically, and the choice can change between deployments. Ties should be rejected or resolved by an explicit rule.

findings.title: AuthzClient.create initialises the process-wide crypto singleton with a stub provider
findings.body: CryptoIntegration.init is process-global and only runs once. If an application calls AuthzClient.create() before any other crypto initialisation, and only the authz-client jar (with AuthzClientCryptoProvider, order 100) is on the classpath, the singleton becomes AuthzClientCryptoProvider. Most of its methods throw UnsupportedOperationException. Later calls to CryptoIntegration.init with the real provider are then no-ops, so the stub stays in place for the whole JVM and other code fails at runtime.

findings.title: Oversized r/s integers are silently truncated when converting DER to concatenated form
findings.body: In asn1derToConcatenatedRS, integerToBytes(rBigInteger, len) drops the high-order bytes when the decoded integer is longer than len. The input DER comes from an externally supplied signature. A value that does not fit in the curve's field size should be rejected, but here it is silently reduced to a different number and the resulting signature is passed on to verification. Values with bit length above the field size, and negative values, should raise an IOException.

findings.title: Malformed length produces NegativeArraySizeException instead of an IOException
findings.body: read(int length) allocates `new byte[length]` without checking the value. readLength returns -1 for the indefinite-length form (0x80), and readNext then passes an adjusted length into read(). Malformed or indefinite-length DER therefore throws an unchecked NegativeArraySizeException from the signature-parsing path, not the IOException the callers handle. Negative lengths should be rejected up front.

findings.title: Dead ASN1Encoder calls in concatenatedRSToASN1DER
findings.body: Lines 114-115 create two ASN1Encoder instances, write the BigIntegers into them, and discard the results. The return statement on lines 117-121 builds the output from separate encoder instances, so these two lines have no effect. They should be removed; as written they suggest the encoding is being done twice or that the code is incomplete.

findings.title: Test only checks round-trip consistency, not that the DER output is valid
findings.body: The test converts the JCA signature to concatenated form and back to DER, then compares the two concatenated forms. It never checks that concatenatedRSToASN1DER produces DER that the JDK's Signature.verify accepts, and it never checks the DER structure itself. A bug that produced consistently wrong but self-inverse encoding (for example, a wrong sign byte on r or s) would pass. The test should verify the re-encoded DER signature against the public key with the JCA. It also does not cover the edge cases of high-bit r/s values or short signatures.

findings.title: getBouncyCastleProvider returns the default KeyStore's provider, not a BouncyCastle provider
findings.body: The method creates a KeyStore of the default type and returns its provider. That is usually the JDK's SUN or SunJSSE provider, not BouncyCastle. Callers that expect the BC provider (for example, to register or look up a provider by name) get an unrelated provider with no error. Returning null or throwing UnsupportedOperationException, as the other unsupported methods do, would be clearer.
